newsitem.title: USA: Niagara Mowhawk investment-grade by 2000? Possibly.
newsitem.headline: Niagara Mowhawk investment-grade by 2000? Possibly.

text.p: Niagara Mohawk Power Corp's yearning for investment grade status is aggressive but also obtainable despite its plan to sell $3.2 billion of new debt in a restructuring plan, fixed-income analysts said.

Chief Executive Officer William Davis said Niagara Mohawk's plan to restructure or terminate 44 above-market cost power contracts will allow it to seek an investment grade rating on its senior debt by the year 2000. The plan, announced on Monday, will be paid for with the additional debt and $400 million in cash.
The issuance of 46 million common shares representing about 25 percent of the anticipated fully diluted stock is also included in the tentative deal, the company said.

Investment grade status for the bonds is within reach, analysts said, based on the improved financial profile of Niagara Mohawk and its delivery from the expensive contracts equal to 90 percent of above-market costs.

"Despite the fact there is substantial debt there is also substantial cash flow suitable for refinancing the debt," said John Spellman, utilities analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "We've also gone from a situation where the company went from an ever increasing liability in the form of payments to a defineable number which can be amortized down in time."
The company indicated in its conference call to analysts that the debt would be amortized over a seven-year time frame, Spellman said.

Susan Abbott, a managing director of Moody's Investors Service utility ratings group, acknowledged an investment grade rating by the year 2000 was an aggressive goal -- but not impossible. Niagara Mohawk's status as the lowest cost producer in the region will help its competitive position, Abbott said, while the political environment appears more favorable for utilities than not.
Moody's rates Niagara Mohawk senior secured debt Ba3. Standard & Poor's rates the same debt BB-minus.

One instrumental piece of legislation would be an approval of stranded asset cost securitization, Abbott said. Niagara Mohawk in its plan would produce further savings for residential and commercial customers.
"If the state says okay (on asset securitization), NIMO may be able to get some support on that," Abbott said.
Standard & Poor's, which on Monday revised its rating outlook to positive from stable, also said New York State approval of asset securitization is a key ingredient to a near-term upgrade.

The agency, in fact, stated flat out that it "does not expect the senior secured debt ratings of Niagara Mohawk to achieve an investment grade rating for several years..." but the higher status would become a stronger possibility with the approval of securitization.

In any event, the savings against what the company would be paying for the independent power contracts is quite large. The $3.6 billion price tag, in fact, pales next to the high end estimates of $9 billion in potential future obligations to IPPs, Spellman said.

S&P analyst Richard Cortwright concurred, noting that the decrease in purchase power expense and the benefit of sizeable tax-loss carryforwards are expected to result in improved cash coverage to interest.

"The potential is now there to remove a huge uncertainty that's been hovering over everything," he said. "If they can wrap these deals up, it's great because the (potential) bankruptcy has been put to rest and the guys have a chance of competing in the open market."
Niagara Mohawk estimates it will save $5 billion, in nominal dollars, over 15 years, with those savings occuring in the second half of that period.
The Street also appeared sanguine on the credit on Monday with spreads of outstanding debt tightening more than 20 basis points in spots, according to traders.
